MODELS AND NODES USED IN THIS WORKFLOW

 Load Diffusion Model

Download ming_image_0.1_design_int8_convrot.safetensors5.75 GB  

Place in: ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models/ming

Create the ming folder if it does not exist.

More versions Ming Image model card 

 Load CLIP

Download ming_image_0.1_ling_mini_2.0_int8_convrot.safetensors18.17 GB  

Place in: ComfyUI/models/text_encoders

This is the big file: the text encoder is three times the size of the image model.

 Load VAE

Download ming_image_vae_bf16.safetensors242 MB  

Place in: ComfyUI/models/vae

 Load CLIP - Prompt Writer

Download qwen3.8_27b_w4a8.safetensors16.1 GB  

Place in: ComfyUI/models/text_encoders

The language model that writes the prompt from your idea. It is the one Ming's makers name for this job, and ComfyUI's own Ming template uses it too. It only writes the prompt: Ming still draws the picture.

A smaller writer, if the big one is too much for your computer:

Download qwen3.5_9b_int8_convrot.safetensors11.4 GB  

Place in: ComfyUI/models/text_encoders

Then pick it in Load CLIP - Prompt Writer instead. Nothing else changes: the same instructions work with it. In the tests it kept every word right too, in about half the time; its layouts were a little less tidy.

 License: MIT, commercial use allowed

Ming Image 0.1 Design is released by inclusionAI (Ant Group) under the MIT License. You can use what it makes for your own work and for commercial work.

READ LICENSE 

 After placing the files, restart ComfyUI or refresh model lists using the R shortcut.

 Needs ComfyUI 0.38.0 or newer, the first version that can load Ming Image. If the model fails to load, update ComfyUI.

  • Pixaroma

How to update Pixaroma nodes: the help page has the steps for every kind of install, in the Update the nodes part.

How to update Pixaroma

Join Discord  Pixaroma YouTube Channel

{"version":1,"content":"

WHAT EACH NODE DOES

The colour of a node tells you what kind of node it is. Nothing here needs changing except the blue ones.

 Models to download

Orange. Each one needs a file from the list in the note above.

  • Load Diffusion Model (Ming Image 0.1 Design) - The image model itself, 6B, from inclusionAI (Ant Group). It is made for design: posters, flyers, ads, UI screens, infographics, anything with text.
  • Load CLIP (Ling mini 2.0) - Reads the prompt the writer made. It can only read: it cannot write a prompt itself, which is why the writer is a separate model.
  • Load CLIP - Prompt Writer (Qwen3.8 27B) - The language model that writes the prompt from your idea, wired into node 2. It only writes; Ming's own Load CLIP above reads what it wrote.
  • Load VAE - Turns the finished render into a picture. It works with four channels, red, green, blue and transparency, which is how this model can make transparent pictures.

 The speed node

Teal, above the graph.

  • Model Attention Backend - Set to comfy kitchen attention, a faster way to do the model's attention maths. The Run Times note has the numbers. On a graphics card that cannot use it, ComfyUI falls back to normal attention by itself.

 The numbers you set

Blue, and numbered. These are the only nodes you have to touch.

  • 1. Pick Orientation and Size - The size of the picture. The starred sizes are the 2K sizes Ming lists for this model, and they look best; the others are about 1 megapixel and much faster. 1920 x 1080 is Full HD, exact. The orientation switch flips a size between portrait and landscape.
  • 2. Write your idea - AI Prompt Pixaroma. Type your idea in plain words, and put every word you want written in the picture in quotes. The writer model reads it and writes the long, structured prompt Ming works best with, and the render uses that. The prompt it wrote shows in the node after the Run.
  • 3. Seed Random/Fixed? - Fixed repeats the same picture, Random rolls a new one each Run.

 The helpers

Purple. They run by themselves.

  • ModelSamplingFlux - Tunes the model to the size of the picture: a big picture gets a different noise schedule than a small one. It reads the width and height from step 1. 1.15 and 0.5 are the settings from ComfyUI's own template.
  • Format Text - A core ComfyUI node. It turns the size from step 1 into one line, like Canvas: 832 x 1248 px, and adds it under your idea, so the writer lays the design out for the shape of your picture.

 The render

Green. These run by themselves.

  • CLIP Text Encode - Reads the prompt the writer made, through the text encoder.
  • ConditioningZeroOut - An empty negative prompt. This model is made for CFG 1, where the negative does nothing, but the KSampler needs one plugged in.
  • Empty Latent Image - The blank canvas, at the size from step 1.
  • KSampler - The render: 12 steps, euler, simple, CFG 1, the settings from the model card. ComfyUI's own template uses a chain of custom sampler nodes instead; on the same seed the KSampler made exactly the same picture, pixel for pixel.
  • VAE Decode - Turns the finished render into a picture.

 The result

Dark red, at the end.

  • Preview Image Pixaroma - Shows the picture and saves it to your output folder as a PNG. PNG keeps transparency, so a transparent picture stays transparent.

The dark Run Timer above it shows how long the last Run took. Handy when you are trying sizes against the table in the other note.

","buttonColor":"#f66744","lineColor":"#f66744","backgroundColor":"#2a2a2a","info":{"title":"Nodes Info","icon":"node-v5","color":"#3d7cc9"}}

{"version":1,"content":"

SETTINGS

 What this workflow makes

A design from a short idea, with Ming Image 0.1 Design: here, an infographic with five steps and the PIXA bunny. You write the idea in plain words, a language model turns it into the structured prompt Ming reads best, and Ming draws it. The render is the same as in the Text to Image workflow; only the prompt is written for you.

It helps most on designs with a lot of text: menus, infographics, app screens, event posters. In the tests, an idea typed straight into Ming made up garbled text on an app screen and on an event poster on both seeds tried, while the written prompt kept every word right. On the demo idea, 4 of 4 renders were spelled right with the writer, against 2 of 4 without it.

 Full HD is exact

Asked for 1920 x 1080, Ming makes exactly 1920 x 1080, no trimming. In portrait it is 1080 x 1920, for vertical video.

 Writing your idea

  • Say what it is and the style: a poster, a menu, an app screen, a 3D clay look, a flat vector look.
  • Put every word you want written in quotes, exactly as it should read. A list gets one pair of quotes per item.
  • Say where things go when it matters: the title at the top, the bunny at the bottom.
  • The size is not needed in the idea: the writer gets it from step 1 by itself.

The writer turns your idea into Ming's structured format: a JSON description of the canvas and of each part of the layout, with its position and colours, from the back to the front. After a Run it shows in the node, and Copy takes it, so you can also paste it into the Text to Image workflow and change it by hand.

The writer runs at a low temperature with a fixed seed, so the same idea gives the same prompt. A new picture seed in step 3 reuses that prompt and does not run the writer again. For a different layout, change a few words of the idea.

 Transparent pictures

Ming makes a transparent background only when the prompt starts with one of its fixed phrases, and the writer starts its prompt with the layout. So use the Text to Image workflow for transparent pictures, at a 2K size; its Settings note has the phrase.

","buttonColor":"#f66744","lineColor":"#f66744","backgroundColor":"#2a2a2a","info":{"title":"Settings","icon":"gear","color":"#2a9d8f"}}

{"version":1,"content":"

RUN TIMES

Every number below was measured on a 24 GB RTX 4090 with this workflow and its own settings, each run on a fresh seed with the models already loaded. A different card gives different numbers, but the shape holds: the cost goes up with the pixels.

 How long a Run takes

SizePixels12 steps
1024 x 1024about 1 MP2.6 s
1152 x 864about 1 MP2.4 s
1248 x 832about 1 MP2.6 s
1376 x 768about 1 MP2.6 s
1920 x 1080Full HD, about 2.1 MP5.4 s
1536 x 1536about 2.4 MP6.1 s
2560 x 14401440p, about 3.7 MP, 2K10 s
2048 x 2048about 4.2 MP, 2K12 s
2432 x 1824about 4.4 MP, 2K13 s
2496 x 1664about 4.2 MP, 2K12 s

The table lists the sizes landscape. This workflow opens in portrait, where each size is simply turned on its side, and turning a size does not change the time: 2.4 s for 1152 x 864 against 2.5 s for 864 x 1152, and 12 s for 2496 x 1664 against 12 s for 1664 x 2496.

This workflow opens at 832 x 1248, about 1 megapixel: quick on any card that runs the model. The starred sizes are Ming's recommended 2K sizes. Switch to one for the picture you keep: four times the pixels. Changing the size also runs the writer again (see The writer, below).

 The writer

Node 2 runs a second model before the render: the writer, from Load CLIP - Prompt Writer. It reads your idea and writes the prompt. On this 4090 the Qwen3.8 27B took 25 to 27 s to write the demo prompt, and the smaller Qwen3.5 9B 12 to 13 s. The table above is the render alone, with the prompt already written.

The writer only runs again when what it reads changes: the idea, or the size in step 1, because the size goes into its prompt too. A new picture seed alone reuses the prompt it already wrote.

What you changedWhole Run at 832 x 1248
Only the seed (step 3)3.4 s
The idea, 27B writerabout 36 s
The idea, 9B writer21 to 23 s
The size, here to 1664 x 2496 (the writer runs again)45 s

 Kitchen attention

The teal Model Attention Backend node is set to comfy kitchen attention, a faster way to do the attention maths. On the same seed at 2048 x 2048, it took 12 s, against 18 s with the normal pytorch attention. Both had the same layout and the same text; the details differed, so treat it as a different seed rather than a worse picture. To compare it yourself, switch the node to pytorch attention.

It needs an Nvidia or AMD graphics card. On anything else ComfyUI falls back to normal attention by itself, so the workflow still runs.

 The first Run of the session

The first Run after starting ComfyUI loads the writer, the 5.75 GB image model and the 18.2 GB text encoder. Measured on the demo at 832 x 1248 with every model unloaded first: about 37 s, of which the writer took about 26 s.

The writer comes from a loader, so it stays loaded between Runs. Compared with letting the writer unload itself after every Run, this kept about 6 GB more RAM in use on this PC, and made each new idea about 3 s quicker.

That was with the model files still in this machine's file cache. The very first load after switching the computer on reads them off the disk for real and will be slower; that case was not measured, so no number is given for it.

 Smaller graphics cards

ComfyUI loads this model in pieces, so it does not have to fit on the card in one go. In a test of the Text to Image workflow, which renders exactly like this one, ComfyUI was told to use only about 8 GB of this card and stayed within it, the 2K sizes included. The writer was not part of that test. With nothing limiting it, it took about 23 GB of this 24 GB card: ComfyUI uses the room it has.

That test ran on a 4090, so it shows what fits, not how fast a smaller card is. A slower card takes longer, and a 2K picture takes about five times as long as a 1 MP one. That is why this workflow opens at a 1 MP size.

 System RAM

With the whole card to itself, ComfyUI held 6 to 9 GB of RAM in this workflow. The writer is one more model, 16.1 GB for the 27B or 11.4 GB for the 9B, and it stays loaded between Runs (see The first Run of the session).

On a smaller card the models wait in RAM instead. That was measured for the Text to Image workflow, up to about 22 GB when ComfyUI was told to use 6 GB of the card, but not with the writer added. Plan on 32 GB of RAM at the very least, and use the 9B writer if the 27B is too much for your computer.

","buttonColor":"#f66744","lineColor":"#f66744","backgroundColor":"#2a2a2a","info":{"title":"Run Times","icon":"run-timer","color":"#3f9a4f"}}

aiPromptState.idea: an infographic poster titled "LEARN COMFYUI IN 5 STEPS" with five numbered rows, each with a small icon: "1 INSTALL COMFYUI", "2 DOWNLOAD A MODEL", "3 OPEN A WORKFLOW", "4 WRITE YOUR IDEA", "5 PRESS RUN", and a cute cartoon bunny in an orange hoodie waving at the bottom
aiPromptState.formula:
You are a senior visual designer and image-prompt engineer. Expand the user's request into one precise, high-resolution Figma-style caption. Return only one JSON object: your answer starts with { and ends with }, with no code fence and no words before or after it.

Use exactly two top-level keys. `canvas_settings` contains exactly `aspect_ratio`, `ambient_lighting`, and `image_style`. `layers` lists visible groups from background to topmost overlay. Every layer contains exactly `description`, `coordinates`, `hierarchy_and_relation`, and `color_specs`; `color_specs` is an array of hex colors.

The request ends with a line giving the canvas size in pixels. `aspect_ratio` says whether that canvas is portrait, landscape or square, then copies the width and the height from that line exactly, in pixels; do not work out a ratio. Lay out every layer for that shape, and spread the design over the whole canvas the way a finished poster uses its space: even margins, and no large empty band unless the request asks for empty space. Fill space by giving the parts more room or with imagery that suits the design, never with text the request did not give. If no size line is given, choose the shape that suits the design.

`coordinates` MUST be one string, never an object or array, in exactly this form: `"cx: 0.500, cy: 0.500, w: 1.000, h: 1.000"`. Values are normalized; each bbox encloses its complete owned object and stays inside the canvas.

A layer is one selectable visible semantic group: background, full person, coherent object, panel, card, row, or text block. Prefer the fewest groups that preserve the layout. Keep people and objects intact. Never create invisible parents, guides, placeholders, empty layers, duplicate summaries, or multiple owners for one element. The first layer is the background, and its description says what fills the whole canvas from edge to edge.

Preserve every user-supplied rendered string character-for-character and as one contiguous string. Unless multiple visible copies are requested, it must occur exactly once across all `description` fields and zero times in `hierarchy_and_relation`. Quote it only where describing its visible rendering, inside escaped double quotes; refer to the related subject elsewhere with unquoted semantic wording. Enumerate intended copy, invent extra copy sparingly, and never hide content behind "other text", "remaining labels", or "etc." Every piece of text that will be visible is written out in full, in quotes, in the layer that shows it: the image model draws any text whose words are not given as gibberish, so a list in the request becomes one quoted string per item, and small print you add gets its own words.

Describe concrete composition, typography, materials, texture, lighting, pose, and camera treatment without literary filler. Every description is a full sentence a designer could build from: what the part is made of, its colours, what sits where inside it, and the style of any text in it; the image model fills any vaguely described area with marks and text of its own. Use `hierarchy_and_relation` only for ownership, alignment, containment, stacking, and occlusion.

Infer structured layouts first. Use one complete layer per card and state its row and column. A compact secondary table may be one layer only if every header and cell is listed; otherwise use a visible shared frame when present, one complete header, and one complete layer per body row, binding values to columns and stating blanks. Enumerate sequences, schedules, spans, gaps, and vacant tracks in visual order. Do not mistake ordinary alignment for a table.

Silently verify schema, string coordinates, Z-order, exact-text counts, geometry, bbox validity, and completeness.

The user's request:
